resources.string: Sleevesight reads what your music player is playing, looks it up in the sources you switch on, and has the AI service you choose write about it. Before you start, here is what it reads, and what leaves your phone.
Sleevesight reads what your music player is playing, looks it up in the sources you switch on, and has the AI service you choose write about it. Here is what it reads, and what leaves your phone.

Sleevesight reads what apps say they are playing, to find your music players and follow the ones you switch on, never your notifications, messages or contacts. For that it needs notification access: Android lets an app list what other apps are playing only with this access, which cannot be limited to one app. It checks which players report music (a track with a title and an artist), to list them in its settings by name, and keeps or sends nothing of the players you do not follow. From the players you follow (Spotify by default), it reads which player it is; the title, artists, album (with its year, when the player sends one, shown after it), length and cover; whether it is playing, and how far into the track; and the queue of tracks up next, with its name. It never reads calls from the phone app or sessions Android marks as voice calls, and never touches the audio.
What leaves the phone, and to whom

To the sources you switch on, such as MusicBrainz and Wikipedia (with Wikidata): the title and artists of the playing track, cleaned of tags such as “2006 Remaster”. Wikidata gets only identifiers. For the genre labels, Last.fm also gets the album name, the only source that does. While “Proactive” is on, as it is by default, the title and artists of the next track in the player’s queue also go to MusicBrainz, if switched on.

To the AI service you choose: the title, artists and album, and what the sources found. This is for the playing track only: the next one in the queue is looked up ahead, but no insight is written for it until it plays.
Your API keys: each only to the service it belongs to, with each request to it.
To the server a cover’s web address names, when a player gives the cover only as a web address: a request for that image. The address itself may identify the album or episode.

To your phone’s text-to-speech engine, only when an insight is read aloud: its text. The engine is the one chosen in Android’s settings; some, such as Google’s network voices, send the text to their server to be spoken.

To the developer, only if you send it: a report of a problem with an insight. “Report a problem” shows the whole report, with the track, the insight and its evidence, and the AI service and model that wrote it, and hands it to your mail app, addressed to support@sleevesight.app. It reaches the developer only if you send it; until then your mail app handles it as any message you write, which may keep a draft in your mail account. That report never holds your API keys, history or settings. In developer mode with “Report button” on (the test build’s default), a button on Home does the same for a report of the app’s state: its settings, what it received from the player, the sources and the AI service, and its diagnostics, with the track changes only if you add them; never your API keys.
Each of these services also sees your phone’s IP address, as every service you connect to does.

Nothing else leaves the phone, unless you export the diagnostics to a file yourself, hand a report to your mail app, or type a key on a computer, when the phone advertises itself over Bluetooth to devices nearby. The length of each track, the list of tracks played, and the record of track changes used to tell your skips from natural ends stay on it, and are left out of Android’s backup. Your API keys are stored encrypted and never logged.
No accounts of our own, no telemetry, no crash reporting of our own, no analytics, no ads.
The privacy policy says more, with where Sleevesight stands under the GDPR and the EU AI Act:
In the settings that open, turn on Sleevesight, then come back here.
No settings screen for notification access opened. Look for it under Settings, Apps, Special app access.

Android will warn that Sleevesight could read all your notifications, such as messages; some phones name banking apps, or make you wait before you can allow it. Sleevesight uses the access only to see what apps say they are playing, to find your music players, and follows only the players you switch on (Spotify by default). It never reads your notifications, messages or contacts, and never acts on them or on calls. Android lets an app list what other apps are playing only with this access, and the access cannot be limited to one app. The privacy policy says more, and Sleevesight’s code is open source.

Using this key means agreeing to Google’s Gemini API terms. They require you to be 18 or older, and are for professional or business purposes, not for consumer use.

Insights on the playing track, written by your AI service from the sources’ evidence. Each insight written is a paid call on your AI service key. Stop writing ends the call at once; if the request has reached your AI service, it still charges for what it has read and written so far. Look again, in the menu beside Write insight, looks every source up afresh, a paid search with Exa web search on, and writes nothing; when the sources found something new, Rewrite insight writes the insight from it, a paid call, only if you tap it. When disabled, no AI calls are made; the evidence is still shown.
Select what triggers writing an insight. The arrow beside Write insight, under Key insights, sets it too. Choosing an automatic mode starts automatic writing from the next track.
Stops automatic writing after a number of track changes while Sleevesight is not on screen, counted again from each time you open it. Opening Sleevesight resumes it.

The player’s crossfade, for telling your skips from natural ends under “On track skip (auto)”.
Looks up the next track in the player’s queue ahead, so its sources come sooner when it plays. No insight is written ahead, and nothing is paid for.
Keep Sources as you left them
Keeps the sources under each track’s insight folded or unfolded as you left them on the track before. When disabled, each new track’s sources start folded. Applies with Expandable boxes.

Allows Sleevesight to look up information from sources while it is in the background, for every track played. With Reactive set to On track change (auto) or On track skip (auto), insights are then written, and paid for, whether you read them or not, up to the Stop after limit when Saver is on.

When you play several tracks by the same artist, each insight would tell the artist’s background again. With this on, an insight leaves out what an earlier one in the same listening session already said about the artist, and focuses on the song when there is enough to say about it. A new session starts after a break in listening, set under %1$s in %2$s.
How long each source’s findings are kept
Keep what sources said about each artist

Keeps what MusicBrainz, Wikipedia and Last.fm said about each artist on this phone, so an artist is not looked up again for every track. This keeps a list of the artists you have heard on the phone. When disabled, each track’s artists are looked up again. Each track’s own lookups send its artists’ names either way. Turning it off deletes what was kept.

How long Sleevesight keeps, on this phone, the list of tracks you played, the track changes recorded to learn your skips, and the insights and genre explanations written for them, counted from when each was played or written. Anything older is no longer shown and is deleted. A shorter time applies at once.

A track that starts after a longer break begins a new listening session, counted from when the last track was heard. Earlier sessions stay in your history, for as long as “Keep history for” is set. Within a session, each artist fact is told once, unless “Don’t repeat artist facts” is off. A change applies from the next track that starts.
Delete everything Sleevesight kept about the tracks you played

The list of tracks you played, the track changes recorded to learn your skips, the insights and genre explanations written, and what the sources found are deleted from this phone. Your API keys and settings stay. Your music is not touched. This cannot be undone.

resources.string: Sleevesight is free software, under the GNU General Public License, version 3. What it shows comes from these sources, its text is set in this font, its icons come from this set, the words of Load keys from this list, and it is built on these libraries, each under its own terms.
Recordings, releases, artists, credits and dates, from MusicBrainz.
Genre labels, from the artists’ tags by MusicBrainz contributors. Used for labels only, never sent to the AI service.
Sentences from articles, by Wikipedia contributors.
Facts on songs and artists, from Wikidata.
Artist bios by Last.fm users, under CC BY-SA; listeners, tags, genre labels and similar artists under Last.fm’s API terms.
Web search results, under Exa’s terms of service.
The hand-drawn font of the notes in Home’s guide, Shantell Sans Normal Regular, from github.com/arrowtype/shantell-sans. Copyright 2022 The Shantell Sans Project Authors.
The app’s font, Roboto 3.016, from github.com/googlefonts/roboto-3-classic. Copyright 2011 The Roboto Project Authors.
The icons in the app, such as the cogwheel, from Material Symbols by Google.
The words Load keys shows, which seal a QR code of keys, from the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s short wordlist 2, at eff.org/dice, unchanged.
The open-source code the app is built on, by licence. Each licence asks that its text, and some the library’s copyright notice, go with every copy of the app: each is here in full.
